posts.text:
The Kremlin wants its ability to devastate a neighbouring country to give it the right to decide how the whole of Europe should live. The meeting between Putin, Trump and Xi Jinping in Shenzhen on 19 November has brought this into sharper focus. Russia’s demands have long extended beyond the Ukrainian territories it has seized. Moscow wants European countries to have to seek its approval for their decisions. Russia sees Europe as part of its sphere of influence.

In Russia’s vision of a multipolar world, states have different rights. A handful of major powers decide how the world should be organised and determine their neighbours’ futures. The rest are allowed only as much autonomy as the stronger power permits. A country may have its own government, hold elections and call itself independent. But its freedom ends where Moscow declares its “special interests”.

Moscow has long offered Europe a place in an order it considers right. As early as 27 October 2022, Putin stated: “Greater Eurasia could also naturally include its western tip—Europe.” He attributed European leaders’ reluctance to participate to their belief in their own superiority. On 22 August 2026, Lavrov continued this line of argument with the words “When the western part of the continent comes to its senses…”, linking Europe’s participation in the Eurasian project to the election of politicians who would abandon the course set by the Brussels bureaucracy. Europeans are offered autonomy on condition that their choices suit Moscow.

Propagandists describe this future more openly. In January 2026, Karaganov predicted that some European countries would join “Greater Eurasia” by around 2035, welcomed Europe’s disintegration and advocated military coercion, including with nuclear weapons. In August, Ishchenko argued that Europe would benefit from Ukraine’s defeat if it realigned with Russia in time, gaining economic advantages and protection from two nuclear powers.

Meanwhile, Europeans are being told that their voice no longer matters. Even before the summit, RIA Novosti columnist Pyotr Akopov declared it historic, regardless of what the participants might agree on. After the meeting, Yuri Baranchik published an article with the revealing title “Shenzhen: The Great Powers Make Deals, Everyone Else Pays”. He presented the Europeans’ absence as proof that their security could be discussed without them. Europeans are being asked to believe that their fate has already been decided, so there is no point in resisting.

Russia’s official demands follow the same logic. After talks with US representatives on 12 November, Yuri Ushakov reiterated Moscow’s conditions: no further NATO enlargement, limits on weapons deployments near Russia, and a return to the Alliance’s force posture at the time of the signing of the 1997 NATO–Russia Founding Act. This directly affects the defence of countries that have long been NATO members.

Sergei Ryabkov’s statement on 20 November shows just how far these demands go. Asked about Ukraine joining the EU, he said that Moscow no longer saw any significant difference between the European Union and NATO. He linked the acceptability of Ukrainian membership to whether it would ensure Russia’s security. The Kremlin is therefore claiming the right to decide even whether Ukraine can join the EU. The idea of “indivisible security” becomes a convenient justification: Russia decides for itself what constitutes a threat, and its neighbours are expected to adjust. Under this logic, any neighbour becoming stronger and more independent can be declared a threat.

Moscow also proposes rebuilding the security system itself to accommodate these demands. In his speech on 3 November, Sergei Lavrov promoted a Eurasian security architecture as an alternative to the Euro-Atlantic order. European alliances stand in the way of Moscow’s efforts to pressure each country individually. The weaker these alliances become, the easier it is to intimidate individual states, create economic difficulties for them and demand concessions.

Proposals for separate non-aggression pacts should also be read against this background. On 11 November, Russian Foreign Ministry official Alexey Drobinin suggested that some NATO members could conclude such agreements with Russia and receive individual guarantees. The danger is that each government is being invited to seek its own arrangement with Moscow. This would allow the Kremlin to reward those willing to concede and put greater pressure on those who refuse. Economic offers can serve the same purpose. If European governments begin negotiating separately with Russia over the terms on which it will leave them alone, collective security will gradually lose its meaning. Europe could thus find itself within Russia’s sphere of influence without a single document explicitly saying so.

Propaganda presents all of this as a sensible path to peace. European leaders are portrayed as dependent on others, short-sighted and invested in prolonging the war. Russia, meanwhile, supposedly only asks others to accept circumstances as they stand. Anyone who rejects the aggressor’s terms is then blamed for the continuation of the war. Concessions to Moscow are presented as signs of maturity and responsibility. In this way, responsibility for Russian violence is shifted onto Ukraine and those helping it defend itself.

Yet the published declaration from the Shenzhen summit contains no agreement to divide the world or recognise a Russian sphere of influence in Europe. It addresses the UN, energy, international jurisdiction and nuclear risks. Propaganda is trying to present Moscow’s preferred future as something everyone has already agreed to. This serves a very practical purpose: if Ukraine and Europeans believe that everything has been decided without them, extracting concessions from them will become much easier.

The greatest danger for Europe is to accept Russian threats as normal and buy peace of mind through concessions. A reduction in the intensity of the war in Ukraine will not remove this risk. Negotiations and economic offers should be judged by whether they limit Russia’s ability to impose its will or give it resources for renewed pressure. To determine their own future, Europeans need shared goals, the ability to defend themselves, sustained support for Ukraine and its involvement in the defence of the continent.

On the program of the Russian propagandist Solovyev, a Russian China expert and publicist Nikolai Vavilov analyzes the results of the trilateral meeting between Putin, Trump, and Xi Jinping.

He says that Russia, the USA, and China want to divide the world into zones of their influence:

"I propose we reflect on this right now and actually set some kind of common goal for ourselves - for the Russian track as a whole. The thing is, if China wants to lock in the East Asian zone for itself - that is, through control over Taiwan, the return of Taiwan, and gaining control over its traditional spheres of influence, namely Japan, South Korea, Southeast Asia, and so on - and the United States wants to get the Western Hemisphere, then we, as experts, have the right to talk about this out loud: it would be good for Russia to institutionally secure a sphere of influence in Europe for itself. And you often ironically bring up that Russia must reach Lisbon.

I think that might not even be irony at all. That is, truly, in a new world where Europe is assigned the role of a periphery of Eurasia - it is a periphery - potential control over it in the future should be secured by Russia. I'm not talking about military methods right now; we are not talking about that at all, rather the natural course of events dividing the world among this 'big three.'"
